full_judgment:
Shahidul Islam J: By the Rule, the opposite party No. 1 was called upon to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 4-9-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 72 of 2003 by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Noakhali, dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 30-9-2003 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 101 of 2002 by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar Court, Noakhali, dismissing the Miscellaneous Case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 (ii)	the pre-emptor being a co-sharer in respect of schedule-2 land of the kabala deed sought pre-emption and being not a co-sharer in respect of schedule 1 land to the kabala made deposit of the proportionate amount along with statutory compensation which is in conformity with the provision of section 96(3)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act; 

 (iii)	both the Courts below misconceived the provisions of section 96(3)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and rejected the pre-emption application. 

 Mr Mahbubey Alam with Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party, submitted that the pre-emption case under section 96 of the State  Acquisition and Tenancy Act is subject to satisfaction of the condition as laid down in section 96(3)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He pointed out that there is nothing mentioned in the plaint that the pre-emptor was not co-sharer to the schedule 1 land transferred by the deed under pre-emption and further pointed out, that no sale price has been mentioned separately holding-wise. He submitted that in view of the said fact the pre-emptor had no option but to make deposit of the entire consideration money. He submitted further, that the prayer for amendment of the plaint having been made long after the statutory period of limitation of filing of the pre-emption case that was lawfully rejected. He further submitted, that the appellate Court did not commit an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice. 

 13. We have perused the substantive application for preemption. At paragraph No. 5 of the pre-emption application as referred to by the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor-petitioner that he himself had deposited partial deposit of the kabala money along with partial compensation and sought pre-emption of a portion of land transferred by the kabala dated 27-3-2002 making the following statements: 

 14. On perusal of the said statements it appears that the pre-emptor at the time of institution of the pre-emption case has deposited partial consideration money along with compensation at his own risk and without taking leave of the Court abandoning his right of pre-emption in respect of one of the holdings. 

 15. It is by now settled that partial deposit of consideration money is barred under the provisions of section 96(3)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which reads thus: 

 (3) (a) An application made under sub-section (1) shall be dismissed unless the applicant or applicants, at the time of making it, deposit in the Court the amount of the consideration money or the value of the transferred holding or portion or money of the value of the transferred holding or portion or share of the holding as stated in the notice under section 89 or in the deed of transfer, as the case may be, together with compensation at the rate of ten per centum of such amount. 

 19. On a close and careful reading of section 96(3)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it appears that the pre-emptor was required to make deposit of the entire consideration money along with statutory compensation and the pre-emptor cannot make partial deposit in exercising the right of pre-emption. But in the instant case that has not been done. In the case of Karimunessa Begum Chowdhurani vs Niranjan Chowdhury reported in 43 DLR (AD) 108 as many as 5(five) holdings were transferred by a single kabala and the price of each and every transferred holding was separately and individually mentioned. The pre-emptor sought pre-emption against 4(four) transferred holdings and left out one holding. It was held that since price of each holding was mentioned separately and pre-emption lies holding-wise that pre-emption was held to be maintainable. 

 "Where on a certain day the landlord filed an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and also filed along with it challans for the deposit of the money required but the challans were passed and the deposit of money was made on a subsequent day. Held that the application was in order since the deposit was made within the statutory period of limitation."
